This article covers checking environment dependencies, comparing installation across distributions, the image-download process with waydroid init, the container’s first startup, and end-to-end verification.

Waydroid is neither an emulator nor a virtual machine. It uses Linux namespace isolation and binder passthrough to run Android userspace directly on the host kernel. This brings extremely low overhead but also imposes firm requirements on the host environment. Assess requirements by component: container startup, the graphical session, and application compatibility are separate levels of acceptance testing.
A Wayland session: A firm requirement

Waydroid must run in a Wayland session; it does not natively support X11. This is because the Android graphics stack renders directly to the host compositor through the wayland-client protocol, bypassing the X11 intermediary.

What can X11 users do?
If your desktop environment still runs on X11, such as certain older GNOME versions, Xfce, or MATE, there are two options:
Switch to a Wayland session: In the login manager (SDDM/GDM/LightDM), select a session option with a "Wayland" suffix. This is the recommended approach.
Use a nested Wayland compositor: Start a nested Wayland compositor inside X11, then run Waydroid within it. Common tools include:
cage — A minimal kiosk-style Wayland compositor that supports only a single fullscreen application
weston — A full-featured reference compositor with support for nested mode
A nested compositor adds performance overhead and should be used only as a temporary transition.
On x86_64, Waydroid’s Android system images are built for x86_64, but some key components, such as the libhoudini ARM translation engine, depend on specific SIMD instruction sets.
Check the Binder, shared-memory, PSI, and networking support required by the current version; not every name corresponds to a loadable kernel module.

binder is Android’s core IPC mechanism. Binder has a C implementation and a newer Rust implementation; module names and availability depend on the specific kernel/distribution. You cannot infer a replacement relationship from version numbers such as 5.7 or 6.7. The common module name for the C implementation is binder_linux.
Check the specific distribution and version
Kernels in modern distributions (Ubuntu 22.04+, Fedora 37+, and current Arch) usually include one of the two. NixOS requires manual configuration; see 03 In-depth NixOS integration.

PSI is the kernel’s resource-pressure monitoring infrastructure. Waydroid’s lxc-monitord depends on PSI to detect resource pressure in the container. Check CONFIG_PSI and /proc/pressure/ first; when PSI is disabled by default, enable it with psi=1. This involves both the build configuration and boot policy; it is not a dependency of the Binder protocol itself.
If psi=1 is not set, modify the bootloader configuration:
On the GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX line, append psi=1, then run sudo update-grub or sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg

A missing psi=1 is the most common cause of installation failure If waydroid container start is followed by lxc-monitord[xxx]: Failed to open /proc/pressure/cpu or the container exits immediately, inspect the actual failure logs and check /proc/pressure/. There is no statistical evidence for assigning a fixed probability to this cause.
Inside the Waydroid container, some system services rely on IPv6 for communication, even if the host does not use IPv6 to reach external networks.

waydroid init is the core step in the installation process. It downloads Android system images, verifies their integrity, and creates the filesystem structure needed by the container on the host.

After the images finish downloading, start Waydroid and perform end-to-end verification in the following order.
Waydroid operates in two layers: the container daemon (a systemd service that manages the LXC container lifecycle) and the Android session (userspace, managing the Android runtime).
The role of the container service waydroid-container.service runs with root privileges and is responsible for:
Starting lxc-start to boot the Android init process
Setting up namespace isolation and cgroup resource limits
Mounting the Android system partition overlay
Android userspace operation is controlled by a regular user through the session bus and does not involve root privileges.
Once the container is running, Android still needs to start its session manager, equivalent to an Android "user login".

Shutdown order
Stop the session before stopping the container. If you stop the container while the session is still running, the D-Bus session manager repeatedly attempts to reconnect, flooding the logs and causing abnormal resource usage.
